stories.title: Myanmar air strike on monastery kills 14: Witnesses
stories.summary: It was not immediately possible to contact the Myanmar military for comment.
article_sentences: A Myanmar military air strike killed 14 civilians at a monastery during a Buddhist Lent meditation retreat in Sagaing region.
The victims were mostly elderly, aged between 50 and 70, and the attack was described as intentional by rebel witnesses.
UN investigators recently accused Myanmar’s military of deliberate aerial attacks on civilians.
A Myanmar military air strike on a monastery where civilians were gathered for a meditation retreat marking Buddhist Lent killed 14 people, two rebel fighters who witnessed the aftermath said.
Myanmar has been consumed by civil war since the military staged a 2021 coup ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and detaining the Nobel Peace Prize laureate.
Over the past five years, more than 100,000 people are estimated to have been killed across all sides as the military battles an array of pro-democracy and ethnic minority rebels.

The Aug 21 attack hit a monastery hall around 9am (10.30am Singapore time) in Myaung township of central Sagaing region, killing 11 men and three women, Nway Oo Myaung, a pro-democracy rebel who helped clear bodies.
“Older people had entered the meditation centre for three months” to mark the period of Buddhist Lent, which roughly coincides with Myanmar’s rainy season, he said on Aug 21.
“Those who were killed, their ages were between 50 and 70,” he added.
“It wasn’t a mistaken target, they intentionally attacked a monastery.”
It was not immediately possible to contact the Myanmar military for comment.
A second local opposition fighter, speaking on condition of anonymity, said on Aug 22: “Five dead people were from our village and the other nine were from other villages.”

stories.title: Manchester City preview: Five key questions heading into 2026-27 season
stories.summary: Enzo Maresca faces the formidable challenge of following the legendary manager Pep Guardiola as new season starts. For the first time in a decade, Manchester City head into a season without manager Pep Guardiola on the touchline. The Spaniard’s departure closes the most successful chapter in the club’s history, a period that delivered six Premier League titles, a Champions League crown and transformed City into the dominant force in English football. His successor, Enzo Maresca, inherits a squad led by Norway striker Erling Haaland and packed with elite talent, but faces the formidable challenge of following a legendary manager. As City kick off their league campaign at home to Bournemouth on Sunday, here are the five biggest questions for the new season. How does Maresca succeed Guardiola? Maresca inherits a club that has been shaped entirely around one manager’s philosophy for a decade. Pundits have already drawn comparisons to Manchester United’s unravelling after Sir Alex Ferguson left in 2013. Maresca was Guardiola’s assistant during the treble season and has since built his own reputation at Leicester and Chelsea, so his appointment is not a total leap of faith. The attraction of Maresca is continuity – City have not sought a radical departure from Guardiola’s football philosophy. The expectation is that City will look familiar in possession, but Maresca must also establish his own identity quickly. He’s also known for occasionally falling out with players and staff, which adds a layer of risk to a job that already involves managing enormous expectations with a squad that finished as runners-up last season.

stories.title: Major Japan defence firms stepping up drone development
stories.summary: The push reflects a global race to develop drones.
article_sentences: Major Japanese defence firms like Mitsubishi Heavy Industries are rapidly developing drones, including interceptor models, to enhance Japan's defence capabilities using advanced technology and battlefield data.
Partnerships between defence contractors and civilian drone makers face public scrutiny, affecting acceptance of unmanned warfare amid concerns over civilian harm and infrastructure damage.
The Japanese government supports adopting private-sector technology for defence, as seen in the 2026 defence white paper, promoting innovation to strengthen the country's defence industrial base.

Major Japanese defence companies such as Mitsubishi Heavy Industries are stepping up their development of drones as the government seeks to make unmanned systems and artificial intelligence a central part of its new defence strategy.
The push reflects a global race to develop drones, whose role in warfare has expanded dramatically since Russia invaded Ukraine.
But their growing use has also raised concerns over civilian casualties and damage to critical infrastructure.
In Japan, partnerships between defence contractors and civilian drone makers have come under scrutiny, putting public acceptance of the industry’s shift toward unmanned warfare in question.
Mitsubishi Heavy said in May that it had developed a prototype interceptor drone capable of shooting down incoming attack drones.
“We developed it in just three months through close collaboration between our research and business divisions,” Mitsubishi Heavy President Eisaku Ito said.
The company can move to mass production faster than startups by drawing on its existing expertise, including helicopter technology, he said.
Kawasaki Heavy Industries is working with European aircraft maker Airbus SE on an unmanned aircraft equipped with Kawasaki Heavy’s submarine-detection and monitoring system.
The companies are considering pitching the system to the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force.
